title: Book Three (1805) — Chapter 5
paragraphs: They all went their separate ways, but except for Anatole, who fell asleep the moment he hit the pillow, everyone lay awake for a long time that night.

"Is he really going to be my husband, this stranger who is so kind — yes, kind, that's the most important thing," thought Princess Mary. Then a fear she rarely experienced came over her. She was afraid to look behind her — it felt as though someone was standing there behind the screen in the dark corner. And that someone was the devil — and he was also this man with the white forehead, black eyebrows, and red lips.
She rang for her maid and asked her to sleep in her room.

Mademoiselle Bourienne paced the conservatory for a long time that evening, waiting in vain for someone, alternately smiling at imaginary encounters and working herself up to tears with the imagined words of her poor mother scolding her for her moral downfall.

The little princess complained to her maid that the bed was badly made. She couldn't get comfortable lying on her stomach or on her side. Every position felt awkward and unbearable, and the weight of her pregnancy bothered her more than ever because Anatole's presence had vividly reminded her of the time when she wasn't like this, when everything was light and carefree. She sat in an armchair in her dressing jacket and nightcap while Katie, sleepy and disheveled, beat and turned the heavy feather mattress for the third time, muttering to herself.
"I told you it was all lumps and holes!" the little princess repeated. "I'd love to fall asleep — it's not my fault!" Her voice quivered like a child about to cry.

The old prince couldn't sleep either. Tikhon, half asleep, heard him pacing angrily and snorting. The old prince felt as if he'd been insulted through his daughter. The insult stung all the more because it wasn't directed at him personally, but at his daughter, whom he loved more than himself. He kept telling himself he would think the whole matter through carefully and decide what was right, but instead he only got more and more worked up.

"The first man who comes along — she forgets her father and everything else, runs upstairs and does her hair and wags her tail and becomes a different person! Happy to throw her father over! And she knew I'd notice. Hmph... hmph... hmph! And can't I see that idiot only had eyes for Bourienne — I'll have to get rid of her. And how is it she doesn't have enough pride to see it? If she has no pride for her own sake, she should at least have some for mine! She needs to be shown that this fool thinks nothing of her and only looks at Bourienne. No, she has no pride... but I'll show her..."

The old prince knew that if he told his daughter she was mistaken, that Anatole was really interested in Mademoiselle Bourienne, it would wound Princess Mary's self-esteem, and his own goal — not to be separated from her — would be achieved. Calming himself with this thought, he called Tikhon and began to undress.

"What the devil brought them here?" he thought, while Tikhon pulled the nightshirt over his dried-up old body and gray-haired chest. "I never invited them. They came to disrupt my life — and there isn't much of it left."
"Devil take them!" he muttered while his head was still covered by the shirt.
Tikhon knew his master's habit of sometimes thinking aloud, so he met the angry, questioning expression on the face that emerged from the shirt with an unchanged look.
"Have they gone to bed?" the prince asked.
Tikhon, like all good valets, instinctively sensed the direction of his master's thoughts. He guessed the question was about Prince Vasili and his son.
"They've retired and put out their lights, your excellency."
"No good... no good..." the prince said quickly, and thrusting his feet into his slippers and his arms into his dressing gown, he went to the couch where he slept.

Although no words had passed between Anatole and Mademoiselle Bourienne, they understood each other perfectly regarding the first act of their romance, up to the appearance of the poor mother. They understood they had much to say to each other in private and had been looking for a chance to meet alone since morning. When Princess Mary went to her father's room at the usual hour, Mademoiselle Bourienne and Anatole met in the conservatory.

Princess Mary approached the door of the study with particular dread. It seemed to her that not only did everyone know her fate would be decided that day, but that they also knew what she thought about it. She read this in Tikhon's face and in the face of Prince Vasili's valet, who gave her a deep bow when she passed him in the corridor carrying hot water.

The old prince was unusually gentle and attentive in his treatment of his daughter that morning. Princess Mary knew this painstaking manner well. His face wore that expression when his dry hands clenched in frustration at her not understanding an arithmetic problem, when he would get up from his chair and walk away, repeating the same words in a low voice several times.
He came straight to the point, treating her with a forced formality.

"I've received a proposal concerning you," he said with an unnatural smile. "I expect you've guessed that Prince Vasili didn't come here and bring his pupil" — for some reason Prince Bolkonsky referred to Anatole as a 'pupil' — "just to admire my beautiful eyes. Last night a proposal was made on your behalf, and as you know my principles, I'm leaving the decision to you."
"How should I understand you, Father?" said the princess, growing pale and then blushing.

"What do you mean, how?" her father cried angrily. "Prince Vasili has taken a liking to you as a daughter-in-law and is proposing on his pupil's behalf. That's what there is to understand! 'How should I understand?' ... I'm the one asking you!"
"I don't know what you think, Father," the princess whispered.
"Me? What about me? Leave me out of this. I'm not the one getting married. What about you? That's what I want to know."

The princess could see that her father disapproved, but at that moment the thought struck her that her fate would be decided now or never. She lowered her eyes to avoid his gaze, under which she felt she could only submit out of habit rather than think clearly, and said: "I only want to do your will, but if I had to express my own wish..." She didn't have time to finish. The old prince cut her off.
"Wonderful!" he shouted. "He'll take you with your dowry and grab Mademoiselle Bourienne as a bonus. She'll be the real wife, while you..."
The prince stopped. He saw the effect his words had on his daughter. She lowered her head and was about to burst into tears.

"Now then, now then — I'm only joking!" he said. "Remember this, Princess: I believe firmly that a young woman has every right to choose. I'm giving you complete freedom. Just remember that your life's happiness depends on your decision. Don't worry about me!"
"But I don't know, Father!"

"There's no need for discussion! He takes orders and will marry you or anyone else. But you are free to choose... Go to your room, think it over, and come back in an hour to tell me in his presence: yes or no. I know you'll pray about it. Fine, pray if you want, but you'd better think it over too. Go! Yes or no, yes or no, yes or no!" he kept shouting even as the princess, as if lost in a fog, had already stumbled out of the study.

Her fate was decided, and happily decided. But what her father had said about Mademoiselle Bourienne was terrible. It couldn't be true, of course, but still it was awful, and she couldn't stop thinking about it. She was walking straight through the conservatory, not seeing or hearing anything, when suddenly the familiar whispering of Mademoiselle Bourienne snapped her out of her daze. She looked up and, two steps away, saw Anatole with his arms around the Frenchwoman, whispering something to her. With a look of horror on his handsome face, Anatole glanced at Princess Mary but didn't immediately remove his arm from Mademoiselle Bourienne's waist — she hadn't yet noticed the princess.

"Who's that? Why? Wait a moment!" Anatole's face seemed to say. Princess Mary stared at them in silence. She couldn't make sense of it. Finally Mademoiselle Bourienne let out a scream and ran off. Anatole bowed to Princess Mary with a cheerful smile, as if inviting her to laugh at this strange scene, then shrugged his shoulders and walked toward the door leading to his own rooms.

An hour later, Tikhon came to summon Princess Mary to the old prince, adding that Prince Vasili was there too. When Tikhon arrived, Princess Mary was sitting on the sofa in her room, holding the weeping Mademoiselle Bourienne in her arms and gently stroking her hair. The princess's beautiful eyes, with all their former calm radiance, looked at Mademoiselle Bourienne's pretty face with tender affection and pity.
"No, Princess, I've lost your love forever!" said Mademoiselle Bourienne.
"Why? I love you more than ever," said Princess Mary, "and I will try to do everything I can for your happiness."
"But you must despise me. You, who are so pure, can never understand being swept away by passion. Oh, my poor mother..."
"I understand completely," Princess Mary answered with a sad smile. "Calm yourself, dear. I'll go to my father." And she went out.

Prince Vasili was sitting there with one leg thrown high over the other, a snuffbox in his hand, wearing a smile of deep emotion on his face, as if moved to his very core yet laughing at his own sentimentality. When Princess Mary entered, he hurriedly took a pinch of snuff.

"Ah, my dear, my dear!" he began, rising and taking both her hands. Then, sighing, he added: "My son's fate is in your hands. Decide, my dear, good, gentle Marie, whom I have always loved as a daughter!"
He stepped back, and a real tear appeared in his eye.

"Hmph... hmph..." Prince Bolkonsky snorted. "The prince here is making you a proposal on behalf of his pupil — I mean, his son. Do you or do you not wish to become the wife of Prince Anatole Kuragin? Answer: yes or no," he shouted, "and then I reserve the right to state my opinion as well. Yes, my opinion, and only my opinion," he added, turning to Prince Vasili in response to his imploring look. "Yes or no?"
"My wish is never to leave you, Father — never to separate my life from yours. I don't want to marry," she answered firmly, looking at Prince Vasili and then at her father with her beautiful eyes.

"Nonsense! Rubbish! Nonsense, nonsense, nonsense!" Prince Bolkonsky cried, frowning and seizing his daughter's hand. He didn't kiss it but simply pressed his forehead against hers and squeezed her hand so hard that she winced and let out a small cry.
Prince Vasili stood up.

"My dear, I must tell you that this is a moment I will never, never forget. But, my dear, won't you give us even a small hope of touching that kind and generous heart? Say 'perhaps'... The future is so long. Say 'perhaps.'"
"Prince, what I have said is everything in my heart. I thank you for the honor, but I will never be your son's wife."

"Well, that settles it, my dear fellow! I'm very glad to have seen you. Very glad! Go back to your rooms, Princess. Go!" said the old prince. "Very, very glad to have seen you," he repeated, embracing Prince Vasili.

"My calling is different," thought Princess Mary. "My calling is to find happiness of another kind — the happiness of love and self-sacrifice. Whatever it costs me, I will arrange poor Amelie's happiness. She loves him so passionately, and she repents so deeply. I will do everything I can to bring about their marriage. If he isn't rich, I'll give her the money. I'll ask my father and Andrew. I'll be so happy when she becomes his wife. She is so unfortunate — a stranger, alone, helpless! And, oh God, how passionately she must love him to have forgotten herself so completely! Perhaps I might have done the same!..." thought Princess Mary.
